Owner of 30 Years Lets Go of His Dream Car 1970 Hemi Cuda 4-Speed To Take Care of His Wife
65 photos
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150
The golden era of American muscle cars produced few machines as universally revered or fiercely contested on the auction block as the Plymouth Hemi Cuda. While pristine, untouched factory survivors often dominate the headlines, the cars that lived through decades of devoted enthusiast ownership carry an equally captivating gravitas. This red gem has had only two owners in 56 years.
Some people never learn how many cars is too many cars, because there’s always that one Hemi Mopar that’s just too good to leave behind, because it might just turn out to be “the one that got away,” in a hypothetical future where the car nut simply walks away from Providence’s offering.
Days before acquiring a black 1971 Plymouth Cuda 440 Six-Barrel 4-speed at the Barrett-Jackson auction in Las Vegas (for $363,000), Troy Bergeron of Mopars5150 had his son Davis steer a flatbed hauler across the Mojave Desert toward southern Arizona. The destination was a private garage in Hereford, just south of Tucson near the Mexican border. Waiting beneath a protective plastic sheet was a striking Rallye Red 1970 Plymouth Hemi Cuda that had remained with the same caretaker for 30 years.
That might just as well have been 30 minutes, when it comes to Hemicudas, there are very little details that can take precedence over those two four-letter words (Hemi and Cuda), which some marketing genius over at Plymouth decided to say in one breath, and spell it accordingly on the shaker hood scoop.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 The long-term owner, a 74-year-old lifelong Mopar devotee named Jim, greeted Davis Bergeron standing in front of his two E-bodies, and pulled back the cover to reveal his prized possession. Growing up as a dedicated street racer in Lowell, Massachusetts, and spending decades around New England Dragway and Maine car shows, Jim always viewed the 1970 Hemi Cuda as the ultimate muscle car. Three decades ago, he finally fulfilled that lifelong dream by purchasing the coupe.
(Fine, the E-bodies weren’t muscle cars, but pony cars, as the title rightfully belonged to the B-body band – Road Runner, GTX, Superbird, Charger, Coronet, Daytona – but tell me if a 426 Hemi anything can be considered “muscle” or not).
Jim acquired the car in 1996 directly from its original owner, a Florida collector who reportedly housed 250 Hemi vehicles at the time (I have a challenge for you, waiting at the end of the story, regarding this particular provenance detail). When the current owner took delivery, the odometer displayed a little over 32,000 miles, though the vehicle was essentially a basket case wearing faded original paint and lacking both its factory engine and transmission.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 Undeterred, Jim commissioned a comprehensive rotisserie restoration, investing $100,000 into the build during the mid-1990s. That’s how you make a small fortune while supporting this hobby: you start out with a big fortune.
Because original 426-cubic-inch Hemi blocks frequently suffered from cracking through the main webs, Jim opted for a brand-new Mopar high-performance crate block with high nickel content. Renowned engine builder Larry Shepard assembled the powerhouse, boring and stroking the displacement to 472 cubes while retaining the correct 1970 cylinder heads, intake manifold, the two fours (that’s dual four-barrel carburetors, in case it’s not clear), and shaker hood assembly.
The motor was recently refreshed and carries just 10 break-in miles. Backing the 472-cubic-inch powerplant is a period-correct, non-numbers-matching 18-spline A833 4-speed manual transmission built by transmission specialist Joe Liberty, featuring a Hurst Pistol Grip shifter paired with a Super Shifter body and shortened levers for crisp, short throws.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 The drivetrain channels power through a chromoly driveshaft to a 4.10 Dana 60 rear axle equipped with a Strange Engineering pinion and snubber, staying true to its factory Super Track Pak specification.
While the underside and engine bay were restored to show-winning standards, Jim incorporated select upgrades for reliability and performance. The car breathes through 2-inch Hooker headers feeding a 3-inch TTI dual exhaust system with an H-pipe and 3-inch chrome tips. It rides on 15-inch Rallye wheels, widened to ten inches in the rear, wrapped in meaty drag radials, while stainless steel brake lines replaced the original setup.
Inside the cabin, the Hemi Cuda retains its factory-installed seats, door panels, tinted glass, and dash pad, while the Rallye instrument cluster with its 150-mph speedometer and 8,000-rpm tachometer was professionally refurbished. Though ordered from the factory as a radio-delete vehicle, an aftermarket Alpine head unit was discreetly fitted, alongside a manual hand choke and rear window louvers crafted by Gene Gregory after Mopar discontinued the original factory parts.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 Documentation accompanying the car includes a 1996 Virginia title copy and a 1996 Chrysler Registry report by authority Galen Govier confirming its pedigree. Built at the Hamtramck, Michigan plant on December 12, 1969, this car is one of 284 Hemi Cuda hardtops with a 4-speed produced for the United States in 1970. Factory options included FE5 Rallye Red paint, front and rear elastomeric bumpers, power brakes, hood pins, and a six-way adjustable bucket seat.
Over his 30-year stewardship, Jim never raced the car, driving it only in 15-mile or 20-mile increments to local gatherings and claiming Best of Show honors at New England Dragway. Fueled exclusively with 110-octane Sunoco racing gasoline and showing 40,483 miles on the odometer, the coupe remained his favorite among more than 150 Mopars he owned. Only failing health and the need to care for his wife forced the sale.
The historic significance of the Hemi Cuda stems from its brief production run during the peak of the horsepower wars. Offered strictly during the 1970 and 1971 model years on the third-generation E-body platform, the model was available in two body styles: hardtop and convertible. Buyers could pair the 425-horsepower 426-cubic-inch Hemi V8 with either the heavy-duty 4-speed manual or the A727 TorqueFlite 3-speed automatic transmission. Only 780 did.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 Scarcity defines the Hemi Cuda legacy, as high insurance rates tightened the market. In 1970, Plymouth produced 652 Hemi Cuda hardtops and 14 convertibles, totaling 666 units. For 1971, output plummeted to 107 hardtops and seven convertibles. When new, the Cuda hardtop carried a base price of $3,164, while ticking the E74 code for the 426 Hemi option added a hefty $871.45 to the window sticker.
It wasn’t a cheap Plymouth anymore, it was a money-printing machine for tire companies – there were few other ways to sell rubber more efficiently than to wrap it on the business end of the seven-liter big-block from Ma’ Mopar.
In the collector market, those humble original figures have multiplied on a cosmic scale. Modified or non-numbers-matching 1970 Hemi Cuda hardtops like Jim's Rallye Red example command low six figures. Documented, numbers-matching hardtop coupes trade between $600,000 and $1,500,000.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 The ultra-rare Hemi Cuda convertibles sit atop the muscle car hierarchy, crossing the auction block for sums between $2,000,000 and $3,500,000 as the undisputed crown jewels of Detroit iron. Speaking of which, let’s get back to the challenge I mentioned earlier. Jim said he bought the car in Florida, from a seller who owned 250 Hemi Mopars.
Do you think it’s just poetic license, or was there a real car nut that massive who actually had 2.5% of all 426-Street Hemi cars ever built? Or it could be that Jim counts first-gen hemi cars into this roll call? What’s even more intriguing is the fact that the car’s original title was issued in Virginia. That’s not inconsistent to the Florida sale – the first owner might have registered the car in Virginia, and simply stored it in the Sunshine State.
